name: DreamBox Math
line: DreamBox teaches in lessons with virtual models. In AMP, each problem carries its own hint, lesson and worked answer.
description: AMP vs DreamBox Math: DreamBox teaches in lessons with virtual manipulatives. In AMP, the problem is the unit, and review is continuous.
verdict: DreamBox Math teaches in lessons worked with virtual manipulatives, and its engine picks the next lesson from how a learner worked in the last one [3][10]. In AMP, the problem is the unit. Every answer updates the learner's level and sets the next problem, and each problem carries its own hint, lesson and worked answer.

reasons.title: The problem is the unit
reasons.body: In AMP, everything a learner needs hangs off the problem in front of them: a hint that gives the first step, a lesson with a worked example, a video lesson, the worked answer afterward, and links to the skills it builds on and leads to. In DreamBox the unit is the lesson. A learner solves problems in it by working virtual manipulatives [10], and explicit instruction comes after exploration [2]. The engine then picks the next lesson from how the learner worked inside the last one [3]. Across 55 studies, worked examples improve performance in math [19].

reasons.title: Feedback on every answer
reasons.body: After each problem AMP shows whether it was right, the correct answer and the worked steps. In DreamBox, the engine watches how the learner works and adjusts hints and scaffolding [2]. When a struggle stops being productive, DreamBox says it will show the learner how to do it, and eventually exit the lesson [5]. Across 40 studies of computer feedback, feedback that explains had the largest effect [20].

reasons.title: Help is recorded, not forbidden
reasons.body: In AMP an answer given after a hint or a lesson is marked as helped and does not count as learned. A skill counts when the learner gets it right without help, more than once. So help stays in reach, and each lesson has a guide for the adult. DreamBox asks adults not to help beyond coaching, because the engine would then adapt to the adult's understanding instead of the learner's [5].

reasons.title: Continuous review
reasons.body: In AMP, learned skills come back in ordinary practice, at growing intervals, mixed with other math. In DreamBox, material comes back when the engine sees a struggle: the lesson's progress resets and the learner replays it [4]. We found no time-based review of skills already learned in the help center and product pages we read [1][2][4]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% on the researchers' own test a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks [18].

reasons.title: Work on paper counts
reasons.body: AMP makes printable workbooks for each learner from that learner's own record, with worked answer keys, and work done on paper counts. DreamBox Math has no printable worksheets, and its help center says, "We do not encourage students to use pencil and paper" during lessons [2].

reasons.title: Counting through precalculus
reasons.body: AMP is one program from counting through precalculus, on one map of skills, and each problem links to the skills it builds on and leads to. DreamBox Math covers kindergarten through grade 8 [1]. Its help center calls it a supplemental digital product, meant to support a core curriculum [2].

rows.range: Kindergarten through grade 8 [1]. Its maker calls it a supplement to a core curriculum [2].
rows.start: At home, a learner starts in the upcoming grade and the engine adjusts [8]. Schools can add a placement assessment at the start of each school year [7].
rows.teaching: Inside lessons, worked with virtual manipulatives, with narrated directions and hints. Explicit instruction comes after exploration [10][11][2].
rows.next: The engine picks the next lesson from how the learner worked inside the last one. Adults can steer with Assignments [3].
rows.mastery: Counted in lessons. Some lessons replay with changed content until the learner shows proficiency, and a struggle resets a lesson's progress [4].
rows.review: When the engine sees a struggle, the lesson resets and is replayed [4]. An adult can assign a topic to review [8].
rows.print: No printable worksheets. DreamBox discourages pencil and paper during lessons [2].
rows.adult: Can steer with Assignments. Asked not to help beyond coaching, because help skews the engine [3][5].
rows.reports: Minutes and lessons per week against a weekly target, and proficiency by standard [9].
rows.evidence: Rated Strong by Evidence for ESSA: two randomized studies, grades K-5, average +0.10 [12]. What Works Clearinghouse: potentially positive effects, grades K-1 [13].

theirs: DreamBox Math is an adaptive online math program for kindergarten through grade 8, made by Discovery Education [1]. Its help center calls it a supplemental digital product, meant to support a core curriculum [2].

A learner works in one of three environments, for grades K-2, 3-5 and 6-8 [6]. In a lesson, the learner solves problems by working virtual manipulatives such as a math rack, a ten frame, a number line and bar models [10]. Directions and hints are narrated [11]. The engine watches how the learner works, not only whether the answer is right, and adjusts difficulty, scaffolding, hints and pacing [2]. It then picks the next lesson [3].
credit: Hands-on models. Children build number sense by working virtual manipulatives [10].
It adapts to how a child works a problem, not only to the final answer [2].
Randomized trials found positive effects in the early grades [12][13].

theirs: Evidence for ESSA rates DreamBox Math Strong, on two randomized studies with 13,320 students in grades K-5 and an average effect of +0.10 [12]. The larger, by Lenard and Rhea (2019) in 24 North Carolina schools, found +0.12 on a number test in grades K-2 and +0.03 on the state test in grades 4-5 [12]. The What Works Clearinghouse found potentially positive effects in 2013, from SRI International's randomized trial with 557 kindergarten and first-grade students at three Rocketship charter schools. Users scored 0.11 standard deviations higher on the MAP math test, an improvement index of 4 percentile points [13].

A 2024 randomized trial by Foster compared DreamBox with Zearn among 115 kindergarten and first-grade students. Results favored DreamBox and were not statistically significant [17]. A 2016 study by Harvard's Center for Education Policy Research, in Howard County schools and Rocketship charter schools, found students averaged 35 and 44 minutes a week in the weeks they used DreamBox, when DreamBox recommended 60 to 90. Only 5.8% and 12.5% reached the recommended time. In Howard County, students who used it the average amount gained about 2 percentile points on MAP over similar non-users, and the authors could not rule out other causes [14].

DreamBox's newer studies were commissioned by DreamBox or Discovery Education, and most compare heavier users with lighter users. LearnPlatform's 2023 Arizona study found 0.12 for grade 7-8 users against weighted non-users [15]. Its 2024 North Carolina study had no non-user group [16]. McREL's 2025 South Carolina study found that any use of DreamBox alone did not raise average school-level math scores, while schools with consistent use scored higher [21].
ours: Two findings bear on this comparison. Across 55 studies, worked examples improved math performance, with an average effect of g = 0.48 [19]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders that meets What Works Clearinghouse standards without reservations, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% against 38% for practice in blocks, on the researchers' own test a month later [18]. AMP applies both at every problem.

AMP's own outcome studies are planned: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. The research behind each part of AMP is in our report, and AMP is open source.

them: You want your child to build early number sense by working virtual models, with a program that reads how they work.
amp: You want a hint, a lesson and the worked answer at every problem.
You want to help your child as they practice, with helped answers kept apart from what counts as learned.
You want learned skills to keep coming back in practice.
You want work on paper to count.
You want one program from counting through precalculus.

questions.question: How is AMP different from DreamBox Math?
questions.answer: DreamBox Math teaches in lessons worked with virtual manipulatives, and picks the next lesson from how a learner worked in the last one [3][10]. In AMP the problem is the unit: every answer sets the next problem, each problem carries its own teaching, and learned skills return in ordinary practice.

questions.question: Does DreamBox Math work?
questions.answer: Its randomized studies found small positive effects in the early grades: +0.11 and +0.12 in kindergarten through grade 2 [12][13]. The one randomized test in grades 4-5 found +0.03 on the state test [12]. In Harvard's study, few students used it as much as DreamBox recommended [14].

questions.question: Can a learner use both?
questions.answer: Yes. They are separate programs. AMP places a learner from their first answers, whatever else they use.
